summary: The article examines whether local colleges' intramural sports programs are diverse and inclusive after September 2023. It reviews gender gaps, accessibility for students with disabilities, racial and cultural inclusion, economic barriers, and student leadership, with examples from several colleges. It concludes that progress has been made but asks whether the efforts are widespread and deep enough for systemic change.
one_line: Local college intramural sports are growing and diversifying through co-rec leagues, adaptive sports, cricket, equipment rentals and student committees, but systemic inclusivity remains uncertain.
key_facts: Dr. Samantha Cho, Director of Intramural Sports at City College, reported a surge in student engagement since September 15, 2023.
Maria Gonzales, a sophomore at River State University, said she feels she has to prove her right to be there when playing flag football, a traditionally male sport.
Lakeview University established 'Co-Rec' leagues where men and women play on the same team.
As of September 20, 2023, Lakeview's Co-Rec leagues saw a 30% boost in mixed teams, according to Intramural Coordinator James Peterson.
South Valley Community College started a wheelchair division last October; wheelchair basketball player Wendy Kipling advocates for more adaptive sports.
Eastside Technical Institute launched a cricket league in September, attracting many South Asian students who had felt overlooked by traditional American sports.
Ethan Lane, Intramural Sports Director at Eastside Technical Institute, called introducing cricket 'a game-changer'.
Metro Community College started a sports equipment rental program funded by local sponsors, under financial advisor Thomas Reed, on September 30, 2023.
The Metro Community College rental program has seen significant uptake, suggesting students join more when monetary hurdles are removed.
At Highpoint University, a student committee led by Oliver Quinn has run workshops and outreach programs since early September to widen participation.
The article says progress on gender inclusion appears slow, and not all institutions have adopted adaptive sports programs quickly.
The article ends by asking whether college efforts are widespread and deep enough to create systemic change.
